aeo.what_is: Hallucinations or delusions directly caused by drugs, medications, or toxins, rather than a primary mental health condition.

description.overview: Prominent hallucinations and/or delusions that are judged to be the direct physiological effect of a substance (drug of abuse, medication, toxin) and arise during or soon after intoxication, withdrawal, or exposure. The disturbance is not better explained by a primary psychotic disorder and does not occur exclusively during delirium.
what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life: A college student smokes high-potency cannabis and becomes convinced classmates are plotting against her, checking her phone obsessively for 'proof.'
An older adult on new steroids for arthritis starts hearing voices commenting on her actions and believes the TV is sending her coded messages.
A young man using methamphetamine stays up for days, then sees shadowy figures in his peripheral vision and feels bugs crawling under his skin.
Someone withdrawing from chronic alcohol use hears accusatory voices and sees vivid hallucinations of threatening animals in the hospital room.
A patient prescribed high-dose corticosteroids for an autoimmune flare develops paranoid beliefs that family members have been replaced by imposters.
A teenager experimenting with PCP becomes disoriented, believes he can fly, and experiences terrifying visions that persist for hours.
A chronic stimulant user develops elaborate delusions of surveillance, taping over cameras and whispering to avoid being monitored.
An elderly patient on multiple anticholinergic medications becomes confused, sees children playing in the room, and insists they're real despite reassurance.
common_reactions_to_diagnosis: Relief that symptoms have an identifiable cause and may resolve with treatment
Shame or guilt about substance use and its consequences
Fear that psychosis will become permanent or return
Denial about the role of substances, especially if use was recreational or prescribed
Anxiety about what happened during the psychotic episode and how others perceived them
Confusion about whether they have an underlying mental illness that was 'unmasked'
Resistance to stopping the substance if it served other purposes (pain relief, coping, social connection)
Hope that abstinence and treatment will prevent recurrence

content.diagnostic_criteria: A. Presence of delusions and/or hallucinations. B. Evidence from history, exam, or labs that symptoms developed during/soon after substance intoxication, withdrawal, or exposure to a medication and the substance is capable of producing such symptoms. C. Not better explained by a primary psychotic disorder (e.g., symptoms precede substance use, persist >1 month after cessation, or there is other evidence of an independent disorder). D. Does not occur exclusively during a delirium. E. Causes clinically significant distress or impairment.
content.prevalence: Varies by substance and setting; higher with high-potency cannabis, stimulants (amphetamines, cocaine), PCP/ketamine, and in emergency/inpatient populations.
content.age_of_onset: Any age depending on exposure; often late adolescence to early adulthood for substances of abuse.
content.prognosis: Often resolves within days to weeks of abstinence and treatment. A subset transitions to a primary psychotic disorder, especially with early heavy cannabis/stimulant exposure, family history of psychosis, or persistent symptoms beyond 1 month.

circuitry: Mesolimbic dopaminergic overactivity driving aberrant salience and psychosis.
Disruption of cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loops affecting reality testing and arousal.
neurochemistry: Dopamine excess (stimulants, L-DOPA), NMDA antagonism (PCP/ketamine), serotonergic agonism (LSD/psilocybin), anticholinergic toxicity (antihistamines/anticholinergics), glucocorticoid effects (corticosteroids).
neurobiology.genetic_environmental: Genetic vulnerability to psychosis plus early/high-intensity exposure, polysubstance use, sleep deprivation, and psychosocial stress increase risk.

history_psychosocial: Chronology of use (type, dose, route), last use/withdrawal timing, prior episodes, family psychiatric history.
Triggers (sleep loss, stress), access to substances, legal/social consequences.
medical_assessment: Vitals, full physical and neurological exam; assess for delirium.
Labs as indicated: CBC, CMP, TSH, CK (if agitation/rigidity), serum/urine toxicology; pregnancy test if applicable.
Consider ECG (QTc) before antipsychotics; neuroimaging if focal deficits/atypical course.
standardized_measures: PANSS/BPRS for severity; CIWA-Ar (alcohol withdrawal) or COWS (opioid) when relevant.
risk_stratification: Assess suicidality, aggression, severe agitation, dehydration, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, cardiovascular risk.
differential_diagnosis: Psychotic disorder due to another medical condition (e.g., encephalitis, endocrine).
evaluation.team_and_process: Coordinate psychiatry, addiction medicine, primary care/emergency medicine; involve family/peer supports for collateral and safety.

severity_levels.mild: Circumscribed psychotic symptoms with intact orientation and low safety risk.
severity_levels.moderate: Prominent psychosis with agitation or impaired judgment; functional disruption.
severity_levels.severe: Severe psychosis with danger to self/others, delirium risk, or medical instability.

biological: Family history of psychosis or bipolar disorder
Early-onset heavy cannabis or stimulant use

impact_on_life.social: Conflict, loss of trust, relationship breakdown.
impact_on_life.emotional: Fear, shame, demoralization; risk of recurrence.

psychotherapy: Motivational interviewing and contingency management for SUD.
CBT for psychosis (CBTp) and relapse prevention once stabilized.
Family psychoeducation; linkage to peer recovery supports.
medications: Antipsychotics for acute psychosis: risperidone, olanzapine, haloperidol; consider quetiapine for prominent insomnia/anxiety; clozapine is not first-line.
Benzodiazepines for severe agitation or stimulant intoxication (e.g., lorazepam); avoid if significant respiratory risk.

Treat withdrawal per protocols: benzodiazepines for alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal (CIWA-guided); alpha-2 agonists or symptomatic meds for opioid withdrawal with MOUD (buprenorphine, methadone) for OUD.
Medication-assisted treatment for SUD: naltrexone/acamprosate for AUD; buprenorphine/methadone/naltrexone for OUD; consider bupropion or varenicline for nicotine.
Corticosteroid- or dopaminergic-med-induced psychosis: taper/offending agent when clinically safe; use low-dose antipsychotic short term.
lifestyle_interventions: Strict abstinence from triggering substances; sleep restoration; hydration and nutrition.
Exercise, structured daily routine, trigger/urge management.
care_coordination: Warm handoff to addiction services, IOP/rehab when indicated.
Safety planning; consider harm-reduction education (e.g., fentanyl test strips, naloxone).

treatment_goals: Rapid stabilization of psychosis and safety.
Achieve and maintain abstinence or reduced use via evidence-based SUD treatment.
Prevent recurrence and transition to primary psychosis.
missed_diagnosis_factors: Assuming primary psychosis without establishing temporal relationship to substance use.
Overlooking delirium (inattention/disorientation) as the driver of perceptual disturbances.
Not recognizing medication causes (steroids, anticholinergics, dopaminergics).
overdiagnosis_factors: Attributing psychosis to substances solely due to a positive tox screen without considering persistence >1 month or premorbid symptoms.
Mistaking culturally normative experiences for hallucinations.
warning_signs: Rapid-onset paranoia or hallucinations after use or dose change.
Persistent psychotic symptoms beyond expected intoxication/withdrawal window.
self_help_strategies: Seek urgent care during acute psychosis; do not use alone.
Commit to abstinence plan; attend recovery groups; use craving-management tools.
Prioritize sleep and hydration; create a relapse prevention plan (triggers, coping, contacts).
Carry naloxone if opioids are involved; use harm-reduction practices.

adolescents: Cannabis- or stimulant-related psychosis; higher progression risk to primary psychosis; emphasize family involvement and school supports.
older_adults: Medication-induced (steroids, anticholinergics, dopaminergics); review polypharmacy and anticholinergic burden.

first_person_statements: I thought everyone was out to get me—my roommates, my coworkers, even strangers on the street. After I stopped using and the meds kicked in, I realized how disconnected from reality I'd become.
The voices were so loud and terrifying. I couldn't tell what was real anymore. I was relieved when the doctor said it was from the steroids, but scared it might happen again.
I stayed up for five days on meth and started seeing shadow people everywhere. I knew logically they weren't real, but they felt so present and menacing I couldn't leave my apartment.
Coming out of the psychosis was like waking up from a nightmare. I was embarrassed by what I'd said and done, and terrified my brain was permanently broken.
I didn't connect my paranoia to the weed I was smoking every day. When I quit and the delusions faded, I felt foolish but also grateful I hadn't developed schizophrenia.
During withdrawal, I saw things crawling on the walls and heard people screaming. The doctors kept telling me it would pass, but in the moment I was convinced I was losing my mind forever.

temporal_criteria.onset_timing: Symptoms develop during or shortly after substance intoxication, withdrawal, or medication exposure (typically within hours to days).
temporal_criteria.duration_threshold: Symptoms may last hours to weeks depending on the substance; persistence beyond 1 month after cessation suggests a primary psychotic disorder rather than substance-induced.
temporal_criteria.resolution_expectations: Most cases resolve within days to a few weeks with abstinence, supportive care, and short-term antipsychotic treatment. Prolonged symptoms warrant reassessment for an independent psychotic disorder.
temporal_criteria.recurrence_pattern: Risk of recurrence with re-exposure to the triggering substance or similar agents; a subset may develop a chronic primary psychotic disorder, especially with repeated episodes or early heavy use.

commonly_confused_with.why: Both involve hallucinations and delusions; key distinction is temporal link to substance use and resolution with abstinence in substance-induced cases. Persistent symptoms >1 month post-cessation or psychotic symptoms predating substance use favor a primary disorder.

Delirium features hallucinations, confusion, and altered consciousness, often in the context of intoxication or withdrawal. Unlike substance-induced psychosis, delirium includes fluctuating attention, disorientation, and impaired consciousness. Both can co-occur.

Manic or depressive episodes can include hallucinations and delusions. Substance-induced psychosis lacks the sustained mood episode and episodic course typical of bipolar disorder; temporal link to substance is key.

Both may present with acute-onset hallucinations or delusions. Brief psychotic disorder is a diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out substance causes; clear temporal relationship to substance exposure distinguishes substance-induced psychosis.

misdiagnosis_explained.diagnostic_challenges: Positive toxicology alone does not confirm the diagnosis—many individuals with primary psychotic disorders also use substances. Careful history of symptom onset relative to use, duration of symptoms after cessation, family history, and premorbid functioning are essential to differentiate. Polysubstance use and co-occurring mental illness further complicate assessment.
misdiagnosis_explained.prevention_strategies: Obtain detailed collateral history from family or friends; use structured toxicology panels; monitor symptom trajectory with abstinence; review all prescribed and over-the-counter medications; re-evaluate diagnosis if symptoms persist beyond expected timeframe.

real_life_examples.title: Cannabis-Induced Paranoia in a College Student
real_life_examples.story: Maya, 19, started smoking high-potency cannabis daily during her freshman year to manage stress. Over several weeks, she became increasingly paranoid, believing her roommate was poisoning her food and that classmates were conspiring to get her expelled. She stopped attending classes, barricaded herself in her dorm room, and texted her parents incoherent accusations. Campus police brought her to the ER, where urine toxicology was positive for THC. She was admitted, started on risperidone, and after two weeks of abstinence and treatment, her delusions resolved. She continued outpatient therapy focused on relapse prevention and coping skills, and remained symptom-free six months later, though she struggled with cravings and social reintegration.

real_life_examples.title: Steroid-Induced Hallucinations in an Older Adult
real_life_examples.story: Robert, 68, was prescribed high-dose prednisone for a COPD exacerbation. Within three days, he began hearing voices criticizing him and saw shadowy figures in his home at night. He became agitated and accused his wife of conspiring with neighbors to harm him. His wife brought him to his primary care doctor, who recognized steroid-induced psychosis. The prednisone was tapered, and quetiapine was started. Within a week, hallucinations diminished, and by two weeks, Robert was back to baseline. The quetiapine was discontinued after a month. Robert's family now knows to watch for psychiatric symptoms with future steroid courses.

real_life_examples.title: Methamphetamine Psychosis in a Young Adult
real_life_examples.story: Jamal, 24, used methamphetamine intermittently for a year. During a binge where he stayed awake for five days, he developed vivid visual hallucinations of shadowy people and tactile hallucinations of insects crawling under his skin. He became convinced the FBI was surveilling him and covered the windows with foil. Friends found him in a state of extreme agitation and brought him to the hospital. He was stabilized with lorazepam and haloperidol, admitted for observation, and linked to an intensive outpatient addiction program. His psychosis resolved over 10 days, but he continued to experience cravings and anxiety. He relapsed twice over the next year, each time experiencing milder psychotic symptoms, before achieving sustained abstinence with buprenorphine/naloxone for co-occurring opioid use and ongoing therapy.

real_life_examples.title: Alcohol Withdrawal Hallucinations
real_life_examples.story: Linda, 52, had been drinking a liter of vodka daily for years. When she abruptly stopped due to hospitalization for a broken ankle, she developed tremors, sweating, and vivid auditory and visual hallucinations—hearing accusatory voices and seeing threatening animals in her room. She was diagnosed with alcohol withdrawal and managed with CIWA-protocol benzodiazepines and thiamine. Hallucinations resolved over three days. She was discharged to a residential treatment program, where she engaged in group therapy and relapse prevention. Six months later, she remained sober and symptom-free, though she continued to attend AA meetings and see an addiction counselor.

real_life_examples.title: Anticholinergic Toxicity in an Elderly Patient
real_life_examples.story: Eleanor, 81, was on multiple medications for allergies, incontinence, and sleep (diphenhydramine, oxybutynin, amitriptyline). Over several weeks, she became increasingly confused, reported seeing children playing in her room, and insisted they were real despite her daughter's reassurance. Her primary care doctor reviewed her medication list, recognized anticholinergic burden, and discontinued the offending agents. Within days, hallucinations diminished; within two weeks, Eleanor was cognitively clear. Her daughter now carefully tracks all her medications and advocates for deprescribing when possible.

comparisons.similarities: Both involve hallucinations, delusions, and impaired reality testing; can present with severe functional impairment and require antipsychotic medication.
comparisons.differences: Schizophrenia is a chronic primary disorder with symptoms that persist independent of substance use, often with negative symptoms (flat affect, avolition) and cognitive deficits. Substance-induced psychosis has a clear temporal link to intoxication or withdrawal, typically resolves with abstinence, and lacks the chronic, deteriorating course.
comparisons.clinical_notes: A subset of individuals with substance-induced psychosis may later develop schizophrenia, especially with early heavy cannabis or stimulant use and family history of psychosis. Prolonged observation and re-evaluation are essential.

comparisons.similarities: Both can feature hallucinations, agitation, and altered mental status in the context of substance use or withdrawal; both require urgent medical evaluation.
comparisons.differences: Delirium is characterized by fluctuating attention, disorientation, and impaired consciousness, often with a waxing-and-waning course. Substance-induced psychosis typically involves clearer consciousness with prominent delusions or hallucinations but preserved orientation and attention (unless delirium is also present).
comparisons.clinical_notes: Delirium and substance-induced psychosis can co-occur (e.g., during severe alcohol withdrawal). Treatment prioritizes medical stabilization, identifying and treating underlying causes, and ensuring safety.

comparisons.similarities: Both may present with hallucinations, delusions, mood lability, and impulsivity; both can involve substance use as a complicating factor.
comparisons.differences: Bipolar disorder features distinct mood episodes (mania, hypomania, depression) that persist beyond substance effects, with psychosis occurring during mood episodes. Substance-induced psychosis is directly tied to intoxication/withdrawal and resolves with abstinence, without the episodic mood disturbance.
comparisons.clinical_notes: Individuals with bipolar disorder may use substances to self-medicate or may develop substance-induced psychosis superimposed on mood episodes. Careful longitudinal history and symptom tracking are essential for accurate diagnosis.

comparisons.similarities: Both involve acute onset of hallucinations or delusions with significant distress or functional impairment; both may be time-limited.
comparisons.differences: Brief psychotic disorder is diagnosed only after ruling out substance-induced and medical causes; it is often triggered by severe psychosocial stress and lasts <1 month. Substance-induced psychosis has a clear temporal link to substance use and is not primarily stress-driven.
comparisons.clinical_notes: If psychosis emerges in the context of both substance use and severe stress, careful assessment is needed to determine the primary driver. Collateral history and toxicology are key.

faqs.question: What is substance/medication-induced psychotic disorder?
faqs.answer: It's a condition where hallucinations or delusions develop as a direct result of using drugs, medications, or toxins—or during withdrawal from them. The psychosis is not due to a primary mental illness like schizophrenia but is triggered by the substance itself.

faqs.question: Which substances most commonly cause psychosis?
faqs.answer: High-potency cannabis, stimulants (methamphetamine, cocaine, prescription stimulants), hallucinogens (LSD, psilocybin), PCP/ketamine, and certain medications (corticosteroids, anticholinergics, dopaminergic agents) are most often implicated. Alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal can also cause psychotic symptoms.

faqs.question: How is this different from schizophrenia?
faqs.answer: Substance-induced psychosis has a clear temporal link to substance use and typically resolves within days to weeks with abstinence and treatment. Schizophrenia is a chronic disorder with symptoms that persist independent of substance use, often including negative symptoms and cognitive deficits not seen in substance-induced cases.

faqs.question: Will the psychosis go away if I stop using?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes—symptoms resolve within days to a few weeks of abstinence, especially with supportive care and short-term medication. However, a minority of people, particularly those with heavy early use or a family history of psychosis, may develop a chronic psychotic disorder.

faqs.question: Can prescribed medications cause psychosis?
faqs.answer: Yes. Corticosteroids (prednisone), medications for Parkinson's disease (levodopa), anticholinergic drugs (diphenhydramine, oxybutynin), and others can trigger hallucinations or delusions, especially in older adults or those on multiple medications.

faqs.question: How long does substance-induced psychosis last?
faqs.answer: Duration varies by substance: stimulant-induced psychosis may last days to a week; cannabis-induced can last 1-3 weeks; corticosteroid-induced often resolves within a week of dose reduction. If symptoms persist beyond a month after stopping the substance, a primary psychotic disorder is more likely.

faqs.question: Is substance-induced psychosis dangerous?
faqs.answer: Yes, it can be. Severe agitation, impaired judgment, and hallucinations increase the risk of self-harm, violence, accidents, and medical complications (dehydration, hyperthermia, cardiovascular events). Immediate medical evaluation and safety measures are essential.

faqs.question: Can I ever use that substance again safely?
faqs.answer: Re-exposure carries a high risk of recurrence. Most clinicians strongly recommend lifelong abstinence from the triggering substance and caution with chemically similar agents. For prescribed medications, alternatives should be explored whenever possible.

faqs.question: What treatments are used for substance-induced psychosis?
faqs.answer: Treatment includes stopping or reducing the offending substance (under medical supervision if withdrawal is risky), short-term antipsychotic medication (risperidone, olanzapine, haloperidol), supportive care, and addressing underlying substance use disorder with therapy (motivational interviewing, CBT, contingency management) and, when appropriate, medication-assisted treatment.

faqs.question: Will I need to take antipsychotics forever?
faqs.answer: Typically no. Antipsychotics are usually given for days to weeks during the acute phase and tapered once symptoms resolve. Long-term use is reserved for those who develop a persistent primary psychotic disorder or have recurrent episodes.

faqs.question: Can cannabis really cause psychosis?
faqs.answer: Yes. High-potency cannabis (especially concentrates and products with high THC) can trigger psychotic symptoms, particularly in adolescents and young adults. Daily use, early onset, and genetic vulnerability increase risk. Most cases resolve with abstinence, but some individuals transition to a chronic psychotic disorder.

faqs.question: What should I do if I experience hallucinations or delusions after using a substance?
faqs.answer: Seek immediate medical care, especially if you feel unsafe, are severely agitated, or have confusion or high fever. Do not use more substances. If possible, have someone stay with you and bring you to an emergency room or call 911.

faqs.question: How can doctors tell if it's substance-induced or a primary psychotic disorder?
faqs.answer: Key factors include timing (symptoms arose during/soon after substance use), toxicology results, collateral history, response to abstinence, and absence of symptoms before substance use. If psychosis persists >1 month after stopping all substances, a primary disorder is more likely.

faqs.question: Can alcohol withdrawal cause psychosis?
faqs.answer: Yes. Severe alcohol withdrawal can cause hallucinations (often visual or tactile), agitation, and confusion, sometimes as part of delirium tremens (DTs). This is a medical emergency requiring hospitalization, benzodiazepines, and close monitoring.

faqs.question: What are the long-term risks after an episode of substance-induced psychosis?
faqs.answer: Most people recover fully with abstinence. However, those with early heavy use, family history of psychosis, or repeated episodes face higher risk of developing a chronic psychotic disorder like schizophrenia. Ongoing monitoring and relapse prevention are essential.

faqs.question: Can I prevent substance-induced psychosis?
faqs.answer: Avoid high-risk substances (high-potency cannabis, stimulants, hallucinogens) and polysubstance use. If prescribed a medication known to cause psychosis (e.g., corticosteroids), use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, and report any unusual symptoms promptly. For those with a family history of psychosis, complete abstinence from psychoactive substances is safest.

faqs.question: Should family members be involved in treatment?
faqs.answer: Yes, when appropriate. Family can provide collateral history, support abstinence, monitor for relapse, and participate in psychoeducation. Their involvement often improves outcomes, especially for adolescents and those living at home.

faqs.question: What if I need the medication that caused psychosis for another condition?
faqs.answer: Work closely with your prescribing doctor to explore alternatives. If no substitute exists, use the lowest effective dose, monitor closely for psychiatric symptoms, and consider prophylactic low-dose antipsychotic if the medication is essential. Regular follow-up is critical.

faqs.question: Does substance-induced psychosis mean I have an addiction?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily, but many people who experience substance-induced psychosis do have a substance use disorder. Even if you don't meet criteria for addiction, the episode signals high risk, and abstinence along with evaluation for underlying substance use patterns is strongly recommended.

faqs.question: Can stress or lack of sleep make substance-induced psychosis worse?
faqs.answer: Yes. Sleep deprivation, psychosocial stress, and polysubstance use all amplify risk and severity of psychosis. Recovery involves not only abstinence but also restoring sleep, reducing stress, and building healthy routines.

content.when_to_seek_help: Immediate evaluation for new hallucinations, delusions, severe agitation, or confusion—especially after substance use, medication changes, or during withdrawal.

positive_factors: Rapid abstinence and engagement in SUD treatment
Short duration of psychosis and good premorbid functioning
